question: According to the Vermont CDL Manual, what is a "vehicle emergency" as distinguished from a traffic emergency?
choice_a: When two vehicles are about to collide
choice_b: When tires, brakes, or other critical vehicle parts fail
choice_c: When a driver becomes distracted by shifting cargo
choice_d: When traffic suddenly stops ahead of you
explanation: The manual states that vehicle emergencies occur when tires, brakes, or other critical parts fail, while traffic emergencies occur when two vehicles are about to collide.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17 - Driving Emergencies

question: Why does the manual say steering may be a better option than braking when you don't have enough room to stop?
choice_a: You can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop
choice_b: Steering is legally required before braking in any emergency
choice_c: Steering causes less wear on the brake system than stopping
choice_d: Steering avoids the need for a post-incident vehicle inspection
explanation: The manual explains that when you don't have enough room to stop, you may have to steer away from what's ahead, because you can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.1 - Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: What does the manual say is the best way to be sure you can make a quick turn in an emergency?
choice_a: Rest one hand on the gearshift at all times
choice_b: Keep one hand near the door handle for a quick exit
choice_c: Grip the wheel loosely so it can slide through your hands
choice_d: Keep both hands on the steering wheel at all times
explanation: The manual says that in order to turn quickly, you must have a firm grip on the wheel with both hands, and the best way to ensure this is to keep them there all the time.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.1 - Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: If you're forced to leave the road in an emergency, what does the manual advise about braking?
choice_a: Apply the parking brake immediately upon leaving the pavement
choice_b: Brake as hard as possible right away to stop quickly
choice_c: Avoid braking until your speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then brake gently
choice_d: Never touch the brakes until you are fully back on the pavement
explanation: The manual advises that if possible, you should avoid using the brakes until your speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then brake very gently to avoid skidding on a loose surface.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.1 - Steering to Avoid a Crash (Leaving the Road)

question: What is the "controlled braking" method for stopping quickly, as described in the manual?
choice_a: Applying the brakes as hard as possible without locking the wheels, using small steering movements
choice_b: Pumping the brakes rapidly in short bursts every half second
choice_c: Applying the parking brake first, then the service brake
choice_d: Releasing the brakes completely and coasting to a stop
explanation: With controlled braking, the manual explains you apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels, keeping steering wheel movements very small.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.2 - How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: What is the "stab braking" method described in the manual?
choice_a: Braking with only the parking brake while steering normally
choice_b: Applying the brakes fully, releasing when the wheels lock, then reapplying as soon as they start rolling again
choice_c: Tapping the brake pedal lightly and continuously without full application
choice_d: Braking only with the trailer brakes while leaving the tractor brakes off
explanation: With stab braking, the manual says you apply your brakes all the way and release them when the wheels lock up, then apply the brakes fully again as soon as the wheels start rolling.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.2 - How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: Per the manual, how long can it take for the wheels to start rolling again after you release the brakes during stab braking?
choice_a: Up to five seconds
choice_b: Up to ten seconds
choice_c: Up to three seconds
choice_d: Up to one second
explanation: The manual notes it can take up to one second for the wheels to start rolling after you release the brakes, and if you re-apply the brakes before the wheels start rolling, the vehicle won't straighten out.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.2 - How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: The manual states that most hydraulic brake failures occur for one of two reasons. What are they?
choice_a: Worn tires and low fuel pressure
choice_b: Engine overheating and low oil pressure
choice_c: Loss of hydraulic pressure and brake fade on long hills
choice_d: Faulty turn signals and a dead battery
explanation: The manual lists loss of hydraulic pressure and brake fade on long hills as the two most common reasons for hydraulic brake failure.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.3 - Brake Failure

question: If your brakes fail while going downhill, what does the manual say is your best hope for stopping safely?
choice_a: An escape ramp
choice_b: Shifting into neutral and coasting
choice_c: Turning off the engine
choice_d: Honking the horn to warn traffic
explanation: The manual states that once brakes have failed on a downgrade, your best hope is an escape ramp, and every year hundreds of drivers avoid injury or damage by using them.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.3 - Brake Failure (Brake Failure on Downgrades)

question: According to the manual, what is a sign that a tire, especially a rear tire, may have gone flat?
choice_a: The steering wheel feels unusually light
choice_b: The vehicle thumps or vibrates heavily
choice_c: The fuel gauge drops suddenly
choice_d: All dashboard warning lights turn off
explanation: The manual identifies heavy thumping or vibration as a sign a tire has gone flat, noting that with a rear tire this may be the only sign a driver gets.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.4 - Tire Failure

question: When a tire fails, what does the manual say you should do regarding the brakes?
choice_a: Brake as hard as possible immediately to stop before losing control
choice_b: Pump the brakes rapidly until the vehicle stops
choice_c: Apply the parking brake only, never the service brake
choice_d: Stay off the brake until the vehicle has slowed down, then brake gently
explanation: The manual warns that braking when a tire has failed could cause loss of control, so a driver should stay off the brake (unless about to hit something) until the vehicle has slowed, then brake gently.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.17.4 - Tire Failure

question: What does the manual say about how ABS affects your normal braking capability?
choice_a: ABS always shortens your stopping distance
choice_b: ABS doubles your normal braking power
choice_c: ABS does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability
choice_d: ABS replaces the need for a normal brake system entirely
explanation: The manual states ABS is an addition to your normal brakes and does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability; it only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.18 - Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: According to the manual, the Department of Transportation requires ABS on truck tractors with air brakes built on or after what date?
choice_a: March 1, 1997
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: March 1, 1999
choice_d: January 1, 2000
explanation: The manual states truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997 are required to have ABS.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.18.2 - Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: Where does the manual say trailers display their yellow ABS malfunction lamp?
choice_a: On the dashboard next to the speedometer
choice_b: On the left side, either the front or rear corner
choice_c: On the right side of the rear bumper
choice_d: Inside the cab above the driver's seat
explanation: The manual states trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.18.3 - How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: According to the manual, what is the one exception in which a driver can fully apply the brakes during an emergency stop?
choice_a: When driving a vehicle with no ABS at all
choice_b: When only the trailer has ABS
choice_c: When only the tractor has ABS
choice_d: When driving a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles
explanation: The manual states that if you drive a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles, you can fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop as the one exception to normal braking procedure.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.18.6 - Braking with ABS

question: The manual states ABS should prevent brake-induced skids or jackknifes, but ABS will NOT prevent:
choice_a: Skids caused by worn brake pads
choice_b: Skids caused by low tire pressure
choice_c: Skids caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn
choice_d: Skids caused by an unbalanced load
explanation: The manual's safety reminders state ABS won't prevent power or turning skids caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.18.8 - Safety Reminders

question: According to the manual, skids are caused in one of four ways. Which of the following is one of them?
choice_a: Over-steering—turning the wheels more sharply than the vehicle can turn
choice_b: Under-inflating the tires below recommended pressure
choice_c: Driving with the parking brake partially engaged
choice_d: Failing to signal before changing lanes
explanation: The manual lists over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast as the four causes of skids; over-steering is turning the wheels more sharply than the vehicle can turn.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.19 - Skid Control and Recovery

question: What is the first step in correcting a drive-wheel braking skid, according to the manual?
choice_a: Turn the steering wheel as far as it will go
choice_b: Stop braking, to let the rear wheels roll again
choice_c: Accelerate to regain traction
choice_d: Shift into a higher gear immediately
explanation: The manual says to correct a drive-wheel braking skid, first stop braking, which lets the rear wheels roll again and keeps them from sliding, then counter-steer.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.19.2 - Correcting a Drive-wheel Braking Skid

question: In a front-wheel skid, what does the manual say is the only way to stop the skid?
choice_a: Turn the steering wheel sharply in the opposite direction
choice_b: Apply the parking brake fully
choice_c: Accelerate briefly to regain front-tire traction
choice_d: Let the vehicle slow down by easing off steering and braking
explanation: The manual states that when a front-wheel skid occurs, the only way to stop it is to let the vehicle slow down by stopping turning and/or braking so hard.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.19.3 - Front-wheel Skids

question: What are the three basic steps to take at any crash scene, according to the manual?
choice_a: Call your dispatcher, take photos, exchange insurance information
choice_b: Move all vehicles immediately, direct traffic, wait for police
choice_c: Protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured
choice_d: Turn off all vehicle lights, block the lane, radio for a tow truck
explanation: The manual lists the basic steps at any crash as protecting the area, notifying authorities, and caring for the injured.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.20 - Crash Procedures

question: What does the manual recommend to warn other traffic and help protect a crash area?
choice_a: Set out reflective triangles so other drivers can see them in time to avoid the crash
choice_b: Leave your headlights off so as not to blind oncoming drivers
choice_c: Stand in the road waving your arms
choice_d: Park directly in the middle of the crash scene
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to set out reflective triangles to warn other traffic, making sure other drivers can see them in time to avoid the crash.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.20.1 - Protect the Area

question: Which of the following is listed in the manual as a cause of vehicle fires related to fuel?
choice_a: Under-inflated tires and duals that touch
choice_b: Driver smoking, improper fueling, or loose fuel connections
choice_c: Short circuits due to damaged insulation
choice_d: Flammable cargo that is improperly sealed
explanation: The manual's list of fire causes attributes fuel-related fires to driver smoking, improper fueling, and loose fuel connections.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.21.1 - Causes of Fire

question: When pulling off the road because of a fire, what does the manual specifically warn drivers not to do?
choice_a: Turn off the engine
choice_b: Notify emergency services
choice_c: Park in an open area away from buildings
choice_d: Pull into a service station
explanation: The manual explicitly warns, "Don't pull into a service station!" when pulling off the road because of a fire.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.21.3 - Fire Fighting

question: According to the manual, what type of fires is a B:C fire extinguisher designed to work on?
choice_a: Wood, paper, and cloth fires only
choice_b: Fires in combustible metals only
choice_c: Electrical fires and burning liquids
choice_d: Tire fires exclusively
explanation: The manual states the B:C type fire extinguisher is designed to work on electrical fires and burning liquids, while the A:B:C type also works on burning wood, paper, and cloth.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.21.3 - Fire Fighting (Use the Right Fire Extinguisher)

question: According to the manual, about how much alcohol can the liver process per hour?
choice_a: About one-third of an ounce
choice_b: About one full ounce
choice_c: About two ounces
choice_d: About half a gallon
explanation: The manual states the liver can only process about one-third of an ounce of alcohol per hour, which is a fixed rate that only time, not coffee or a cold shower, can change.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.22.1 - Alcohol and Driving

question: The manual notes that a 12-ounce glass of 5% beer, a 5-ounce glass of 12% wine, and a 1 1/2-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor all have what in common?
choice_a: They are all classified as non-alcoholic beverages
choice_b: They all contain the same amount of alcohol
choice_c: None of them affect blood alcohol concentration
choice_d: They each require a different method to calculate BAC
explanation: The manual lists these three drinks as containing the same amount of alcohol, showing that the source of the alcohol doesn't matter to its effect.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.22.1 - Alcohol and Driving

question: Under the rules described in the manual, when is possession and use of a drug given to a driver by a doctor permitted?
choice_a: Only if the drug is an over-the-counter medication
choice_b: Never, regardless of a doctor's instructions
choice_c: Only during off-duty hours
choice_d: If the doctor informs the driver that it will not affect safe driving ability
explanation: The manual states that possession and use of a drug given to a driver by a doctor is permitted if the doctor informs the driver that it will not affect safe driving ability.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.22.2 - Other Drugs

question: According to the manual, what is the intent of the rules for transporting hazardous materials?
choice_a: To reduce fuel costs and delivery times
choice_b: To simplify paperwork for shippers
choice_c: To contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment
choice_d: To standardize vehicle paint colors for easy identification
explanation: The manual states the intent of hazardous materials rules is to contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment.
source_note: Vermont CDL Manual, Section 2.23.2 - Why Are There Rules?
